response.task_summary: Predict whether an institution’s median student earnings exceed a threshold using pre-outcome institutional, program-mix, selectivity, cost, and student-composition characteristics that should generalize across domain shifts.

ranking.rationale: Business program share strongly tracks labor-market-oriented offerings and earnings across domains.
Health-professions share is a robust cross-domain predictor of higher post-college earnings.
Engineering share is consistently associated with strong earnings and should generalize well.
Computer-science share captures high-return program mix with stable predictive value.
Student academic preparation/selectivity is a strong, semantically meaningful predictor.
Math SAT midpoint is another strong selectivity and preparedness signal.
ACT composite midpoint proxies selectivity and incoming student preparation.
Admission rate captures institutional selectivity, which is broadly predictive.
Instructional spending per student reflects educational resources and quality.
Faculty salary is a stable proxy for institutional quality and labor market positioning.
In-state tuition often tracks institutional quality and expected returns.
Out-of-state tuition similarly reflects market position and perceived value.
Cost of attendance for academic-year institutions captures institutional tier and resources.
Net tuition revenue per FTE is informative about institutional economics and positioning.
Median family income captures socioeconomic composition linked to outcomes, though with some shortcut risk.
Average family income is similarly predictive of student resources and downstream earnings.
Students’ home-zip bachelor’s attainment is a strong contextual SES/education signal.
Median household income from student origins is a robust socioeconomic context feature.
Pell share captures student disadvantage and is strongly related to earnings outcomes.
Ever receiving Pell is a stable proxy for student financial disadvantage.
Federal loan uptake reflects financing patterns and student/institution mix relevant to outcomes.
First-generation share is predictive of student support needs and later earnings.
Public/private/for-profit control is a major structural determinant of outcomes.
Highest degree awarded strongly shapes expected earnings potential.
Predominant degree awarded captures institution type and labor-market orientation.
Carnegie size/setting summarizes institution type in a semantically meaningful way.
Undergraduate degree-seeking enrollment captures scale and institutional type.
Total undergraduate enrollment is similarly informative about institution scale.
Full-time faculty share reflects instructional model quality and stability.
Part-time student share is a robust signal of student mix and expected earnings.
Duplicate part-time share measure remains informative though somewhat redundant.
Average age at entry captures traditional versus nontraditional student populations.
Share over age 23 reinforces nontraditional student composition effects.
Dependent-student share captures life stage and socioeconomic support structure.
Married-student share helps characterize nontraditional student populations.
Gender composition can matter for aggregate earnings through program mix, though with shortcut risk.
Veteran share captures a distinctive student population with different earnings trajectories.
Rolled-up admission rate is useful selectivity information but partly redundant.
ACT English midpoint adds selectivity signal beyond composite scores.
ACT math midpoint adds preparedness information, though overlapping with other tests.
SAT writing midpoint is predictive but less central than math/reading.
ACT writing midpoint is useful but often noisy and redundant.
Education program share is meaningfully tied to lower-to-moderate earnings profiles.
Biological sciences share is informative about academic mix and earnings potential.
Physical sciences share captures academically intensive offerings with moderate earnings relevance.
Math/statistics share is a positive but often small program-mix signal.
Public administration/social service share tends to predict lower earnings than technical fields.
Psychology share is a common major mix signal with moderate earnings implications.
Social sciences share contributes useful program-mix information.
Liberal arts/general studies share is broadly informative about institution orientation.
Communications/journalism share has moderate, stable relation to earnings.
English share helps characterize humanities-heavy institutions.
Visual and performing arts share often predicts lower earnings and distinct institution type.
History share is another humanities program-mix indicator.
Philosophy/religious studies share is informative but usually low prevalence.
Architecture share can be predictive of specialized, moderately high-return offerings.
Engineering technologies share captures applied technical orientation.
Protective services share reflects vocational/public-safety orientation with stable earnings implications.
Legal professions share captures specialized vocational offerings.
Recreation/fitness share is a modest but meaningful program-mix signal.
Agriculture share can matter for specialized institutions and labor-market outcomes.
Natural resources share adds niche program-mix information.
Area/ethnic/gender studies share is informative but usually sparse.
Communications technologies share captures vocational technical offerings.
Personal/culinary services share is useful for identifying lower-earning vocational mixes.
Foreign languages share contributes modest humanities orientation information.
Family and consumer sciences share is a niche but interpretable program signal.
Military technologies share is rare but semantically meaningful when present.
Interdisciplinary studies share offers some information about broad academic orientation.
Theology/religious vocations share identifies specialized institutions with distinctive outcomes.
Science technologies share is a sparse vocational STEM indicator.
Construction trades share captures applied vocational orientation.
Mechanic/repair technologies share is informative for technical vocational institutions.
Precision production share is niche but relevant to vocational earnings patterns.
Transportation/materials moving share adds specialized vocational information.
Net price for program-year institutions is useful but applies to a narrower subset.
Program-year cost of attendance is informative but less broadly applicable.
Program-year tuition helps characterize vocational institutions but is subset-specific.
Distance-only status captures delivery model differences that can generalize somewhat.
Locale is structurally meaningful, though partly entangled with domain geography.
Urbanization degree is useful context but can encode domain-specific geography.
Main-campus flag may matter for institutional structure but is secondary.
Number of branches captures system structure with modest predictive value.
Accreditor may reflect institution type, but can also act as a regional/domain identifier.
HBCU status is semantically meaningful but risks demographic shortcutting and limited transportability.
Poverty rate of student-origin areas is predictive but overlaps heavily with SES proxies.
Unemployment rate adds local economic context but may be more domain-sensitive.
Graduate/professional-degree share in origin ZIPs is useful but redundant with education/income context.
Born-in-US share is a contextual demographic proxy with shortcut risk.
Squared age entry is mostly a redundant nonlinear transform.
Origin-area white share is predictive mainly through demographics and geography, so penalized.
Origin-area black share similarly risks demographic shortcutting.
Origin-area Asian share is a demographic proxy with limited causal stability.
Origin-area Hispanic share is also a shortcut-prone demographic context feature.
Campus white enrollment share may predict outcomes but is heavily demographic and domain-sensitive.
Campus black enrollment share is shortcut-prone and less desirable for OOD generalization.
Campus Hispanic enrollment share is similarly demographic and potentially brittle.
Campus Asian enrollment share may encode composition shortcuts rather than stable mechanisms.
White non-Hispanic share is redundant with other race-composition features and shortcut-prone.
Black non-Hispanic share is likewise demographic and redundant.
Asian/Pacific Islander share is a demographic shortcut feature with redundancy.
Nonresident-alien share can matter but is often a niche composition artifact.
Unknown-race share is mostly a reporting artifact rather than substantive signal.
American Indian/Alaska Native share is sparse and demographic, limiting stable utility.
Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander share is very sparse and likely noisy.
Two-or-more-races share is demographic and less causally stable.
Older AIAN share duplicates newer race-composition measures and is low value.
Older Hispanic share is redundant with newer composition variables.
Undergraduate nonresident-alien share is redundant with degree-seeking version.
Undergraduate unknown-race share is largely a reporting artifact and redundant.
Undergraduate white non-Hispanic share duplicates other demographic composition features.
Undergraduate black non-Hispanic share is redundant and shortcut-prone.
Undergraduate Asian/Pacific Islander share is redundant demographic composition.
Older undergraduate AIAN share is sparse and redundant.
Older undergraduate Hispanic share is redundant with newer measures.
IPEDS region is close to an explicit domain/geography identifier, so strongly penalized.
State abbreviation is an explicit geographic/domain identifier and likely brittle under shift.
Library science share is extremely sparse and unlikely to provide stable generalizable signal.
